entries.title: Co-pilot on Flydubai flight was banned from flying by Oman
entries.summary: The man who stabbed his fellow pilot, the captain of the Israel-bound Flydubai flight, was reportedly barred from flying in his native Oman over security concerns.
entries.content:
October 3, 2026

The man who stabbed his fellow pilot, the captain of the Israel-bound Flydubai flight, was reportedly barred from flying in his native Oman over security concerns.

The co-pilot who stabbed his captain duringFlydubai Flight 1073 had reportedly been barred from flying by Oman over concerns that he had adopted radical ideological views.

The news was first reported by the Wall Street Journal on Friday.

The attack that took place on a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv has raised many questions about how the incident unfolded as well as about background checks in aviation hiring.

There were 182 people on board, including four pilots.

After the co-pilot stabbed the captain in an apparent attempt to crash the plane, two other pilots in the cabin took control and landed the aircraft safely in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.

Flydubai co-pilot was barred from flying by Oman over security concerns

The Wall Street Journal report said the co-pilot was hired by Flydubai despite the ban by Oman, allowing him to fly the jet on a sensitive route connecting the UAE and Israel.

Israel and the UAE, which includes Dubai, signed the Abraham Accords normalizing relations in 2020.

The paper said it could not be determined whether Oman shared concerns about the pilot's radicalization with other countries or airlines.

The nature of his radicalization was also not clear.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Thursday in a video statement that they know the co-pilot "underwent Islamist radical indoctrination" and intended to crash the jet.

Netanyahu also said they were also looking into whether the co-pilot had acted under anyone's direction, warning that whoever was involved would pay a "heavy price."

The investigation is ongoing.

entries.title: US, Australia suspend consular services in Brazil
entries.summary: The US and Australia have announced a halt to their consular services in Brazil beginning Friday. The news comes two days before Brazilians head to the polls to vote in the high-stakes presidential election.
entries.content:
Brazil

US, Australia suspend consular services in Brazil

October 3, 2026

The US and Australia have announced a halt to their consular services in Brazil beginning Friday. The news comes two days before Brazilians head to the polls to vote in the high-stakes presidential election.

The United States announced it was suspending consular services at its embassy and consulates in Brazil due to security concerns starting Friday.

The US did not specify the kind of security issues it was looking at and it did not link issues to the presidential elections in Brazil this Sunday.

The Australian Embassy in Brasilia also said it was closing on Friday, citing the US alert and advising Australians to avoid US diplomatic missions.

The US State Department said it was working closely with its Brazilian counterparts to address security concerns, the Associated Press reported.

What to know about Brazil's heated election

The news comes at a tense time in US-Brazil relations.

Brazilians are headed to the polls this Sunday for what will likely be the first round of the presidential elections that has effectively shaped up to be a rematch of the 2022 contest. 

Surveys show the contest is a statistical tie between left-wing President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who is seeking a fourth term, and right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro.

The elder Bolsonaro, who is a staunch ally of US President Donald Trump, was sentenced last year to 27 years in prison for attempting to overturn the results of the previous presidential election in Brazil.

Trump has not endorsed a candidate, but there are fears that he may be too deeply involved in the outcome of the election results.

US Democratic lawmakers, for example, in late September expressed "grave concern" in a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio over what they said was the administration's "coordinated effort to threaten our strategic alliance with Brazil and undermine the Western Hemisphere’s second-largest democracy ahead of its upcoming presidential election."

Lula and his allies have warned of foreign interference in the election, pointing to tariffs and an effort this summer by Washington to send US officials to Brazil to "discuss electoral integrity."

When asked at the White House whether he would support Bolsonaro in the election, Trump said: "Well, we're looking at that whole thing, and we're watching that election very closely."

Brazil is surrounded by neighbors who've swung to the right and the election outcome — which could be determined on October 25th when the country advances into runoff if no candidate secures a majority of the vote this Sunday — will determine the direction of the country's foreign policy.

Edited by: Sean Sinico

entries.title: Christa Pike unconscious after failed execution — attorneys
entries.summary: Lawyers for Christa Pike said she's unconscious and on a ventilator after a botched execution attempt. Pike is believed to be the first person to have survived the administration of lethal drugs in the modern era.
entries.content:
October 3, 2026

Lawyers for Christa Pike said she's unconscious and on a ventilator after a botched execution attempt. Pike is believed to be the first person to have survived the administration of lethal drugs in the modern era.

Christa Pike was unconscious and on a ventilator in a Nashville hospital in the hours after her bungled execution attempt in Tennessee, her attorneys said in a court filing on Friday.

Pike, who was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, was audibly snoring after she was injected with two doses of lethal injection on Wednesday.

The court filing is the first account of what Pike went through in the hours after the botched execution attempt.

Pike's attorneys said they believed problems with the IV lines caused the lethal drug, called pentobarbital, to flow into her body instead of her bloodstream.

"Apparently at no point did any member of the execution team realize that the IV lines were not correctly placed or that the veins had blown and that the pentobarbital was, in whole or in part, entering Ms. Pike's body," they wrote in the court filing.

Instead of "remedying this failure," they prepared and administered a second dose of pentobarbital, her lawyers said.

Pike believed to be first person to survive administration of lethal drugs

There are now questions about what happens next and whether the state can attempt to execute Pike again given her medical state.

Tennessee Governor Bill Lee, a Republican, temporarily paused the state execution on Thursday, saying there would be a "comprehensive, third-party review" of the case.

Pike, who is 50 years old, was set to become the first woman executed in Tennessee in 200 years.

She is believed to be the first person to survive after being injected with lethal doses of execution drugs in the modern era of the death penalty, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.

entries.title: North Korea fires ballistic missile into sea, Seoul says
entries.summary: North Korea fired a ballistic missile toward the sea off its east coast, the South Korean military has said.
entries.content:
North Korea

North Korea fires ballistic missile into sea, Seoul says

October 3, 2026

North Korea fired a ballistic missile toward the sea off its east coast, the South Korean military has said.

South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff said North Korea fired a ballistic missile on Saturday. 

"Our military detected a ballistic missile launched from the Wonsan area of North Korea toward the East Sea," the Joint Chiefs of Staff said, referring to the body of water also known as the Sea of Japan.

The launch took place at around 6:30 a.m. on Saturday (2130 UTC, Friday), the South Korean military said, adding that the missile flew more than 700 kilometers (435 miles).

According to Japanese broadcaster NHK, the missile likely landed outside the country's exclusive economic zone.

"South Korea, the US, and Japan are maintaining a robust defense posture through close information sharing regarding North Korean ballistic missiles," the statement from Seoul's Joint Chiefs of Staff said.

Meanwhile, the presidential national security office in Seoul called on Pyongyang to immediately halt its repeated ballistic launches, deeming them a "serious act that does nothing to help manage the current situation" and a violation of UN Security Council sanctions.

North Korea slams South's DMZ apology demand

The test came amid heightened tensions between the countries.Land mine blasts injured three South Korean soldiers last month. South Korea and the US-led UN Command have said North Korean mines caused the blasts.

On Friday, ​Pyongyang's Kim Yo Jong, the influential sister of ​leader Kim Jong Un, dismissed Seoul's demand for an apology over the blasts in the Demilitarised Zone, the heavily fortified 4-kilometer-wide (2.5-mile) area between the two Koreas.

Seoul called on Pyongyang to end efforts to fortify the border, including the use of mines and anti-tank barriers.

Kim Yo Jong called those demands "utterly pathetic," adding that the North intended to cut ties with the South.

The projectile launch on Saturday came after weeks of North Korean military displays, including tests of a purported hypersonic missile system, live-fire exercises and the commissioning of a new warship.

Kim Jong Un has also continued to flaunt his growing nuclear program despite US calls to revive diplomacy.

entries.title: UK: Man charged with planning to attack Nigel Farage
entries.summary: The suspect was already charged with the killing of Reform UK's Ann Widdecombe.
entries.content:
United Kingdom

UK: Man charged with planning to attack Nigel Farage

October 2, 2026

The suspect was already charged with the killing of Reform UK's Ann Widdecombe.

A man has been charged with planning acts of terrorism, including against far-right politician and Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, British police said.

"We have been running a hugely intensive and complex investigation for some time," Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans said, saying the investigation resulted in "this very serious charge."

The suspect, Joshua Kerry, was also charged with the murder of former MP and Reform UK spokesperson Ann Widdecombe.

According to the prosecutor handling the case, Kerry allegedly hit Widdecombe on her head 21 times with a hammer while she had been eating lunch.

Widdecombe's murder triggered reactions from across British politics, including demands to improve lawmakers' security arrangements.

The new charges against Kerry include one count of preparing acts of terrorism for actions allegedly carried out between May 31, 2024 and July 8, 2026.

According to the police's statement, the 28-year-old suspect is due to appear in a London magistrates' court on October 7.

Apart from Widdecombe, two other politicians were murdered this decade. Labor's Jo Cox was murdered by a neo-Nazi sympathizer in 2016 and Conservative David Amees was killed in 2021 by an "Islamic State" supporter.

entries.title: New York governor condemns handling of Cornell rape case
entries.summary: An 2024 alleged gang rape at the prestigious Cornell University has gained national attention after the accuser, identified only as Jane Doe, filed a lawsuit. A special prosecutor has been appointed to handle the case.
entries.content:
October 2, 2026

An 2024 alleged gang rape at the prestigious Cornell University has gained national attention after the accuser, identified only as Jane Doe, filed a lawsuit. A special prosecutor has been appointed to handle the case.

New York Governor Kathy Hochul said the accuser of the six Cornell University students of gang rape was "failed" by those whose obligation was protecting her.

This includes both campus police and the county prosecutor, Hochul said.

At a press conference on Friday, she also announced the appointment of Attorney General Letitia James as a special prosecutor to take over the investigation due to the fact she had lost faith in the local district attorney's ability to handle the case.

This came after she learned the "troubling" details of the authorities' handling of the accuser's case so far.

"In what world does the district attorney not even interview her, or anyone else involved, or even request the full transcript?" Hochul asked.

"This young woman had already endured something that is utterly unspeakable. And then at every turn, she was failed by people and institutions with an obligation to protect her."

According to Hochul, the woman, identified only by the placeholder name Jane Doe, told police "exactly what happened to her," including her firm belief that she had been raped.

"Yet, shockingly, those words never made it into the account that the Cornell police sent to prosecutors."

Investigation to take time

Attorney General Letitia James said she did not know how long her investigation might take.

"I know that you want answers. I do too. A comprehensive investigation of this nature takes time, but my office is committed to seeing it through," James said, adding that evidence gathering and interviews will be carried out.

The original investigation into the case was closed without any charges in 2024.

According to Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten, who was responsible for the decision, the woman's sworn statement did not include her allegation of being drugged against her will without any ability to consent and forced into sex.

Van Houten reopened the investigation after the accuser filed a new lawsuit in September, 2026, against seven fraternity members, as well as against Cornell.

The lawsuit has since made national headlines and sparked protests at Cornell and across the United States.

Cornell said it launched a comprehensive investigation and barred the Chi Phi fraternity involved in the allegations, while also imposing a range of disciplinary measures.

The school also said it supports James' appointment and is "committed to an independent external review of all aspects" of its handling of the case.

Edited by: Zac Crellin

entries.title: France: 400 schools closed as student protests continue
entries.summary: Police have made around 2,000 arrests and dozens of people have been injured as student protests spread across France. Ministers have called for a "day of dialogue" but students have called for further strike action.
entries.content:
Published October 2, 2026last updated October 2, 2026

Police have made around 2,000 arrests and dozens of people have been injured as student protests spread across France. Ministers have called for a "day of dialogue" but students have called for further strike action.

Over 400 schools and colleges across France remained closed on Friday as student protests over education-related grievances continued — with some turning violent.

Education Minister Edouard Geffray told reporters that 735 teaching establishments were "affected" in some way on Friday, "30% fewer than yesterday."

He said that three emergency services personnel had been injured responding, again an improvement on "31 yesterday," and condemned occasional "acts of extreme violence" among the wider protest movement.

The protests ​against teacher shortages, dilapidated school buildings and a lack of learning materials erupted at lycées (equivalent to US high schools) in the Paris region last month before spreading across the country this week.

Government ministers tried to strike a balance between empathetic messages to frustrated youth with presidential elections looming, and clear calls for calm in their public messaging.

"Calm must urgently return to high schools and universities," Europe and Foreign Affairs Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said online. "Yes, the right to demonstrate is inalienable. But the violence is inexcusable, and the cynical instrumentalization of youth for political ends is irresponsible."

Some of the roughly 400 schools or colleges that closed had sustained damage amid the demonstrations, with one of the worst hit being the Lycee Mandela in Nantes, which was expected to be out of action until mid-October after a fire in the entrance hall.

Student protests in France: damage, injuries, arrests

Police have made around 2,000 arrests and scores of people have been injured, including 40 high school principals, according to Geffray.

Fires were started in at least two high schools on Thursday, while teachers were reportedly inadvertently ​splashed with petrol ⁠at a third in the southern city of Marseille, according to officials.

At ​least one car was torched in the eastern city of Strasbourg while riot police clashed with youths in Toulouse in the southwest.

In the southeastern region of Auvergne-Rhone-Alpes, authorities claimed that "at least €25 million" of damage has been done in their jurisdiction alone. The Ile de France region that includes Paris estimated damages around €7 million on Friday.

But students have also criticized what they see as a heavy-handed police response.

"You don't want to hear our words; you just fire tear gas," one student wrote on a placard outside the Lycée Voltaire in central Paris.

Minister Geffray told broadcasters on Friday morning that "violent individuals" were "infiltrating groups of students" and "taking the movement hostage" and called on parents to prevent their children from joining the protests.

"What matters now is ensuring our children are no longer out on the streets, because they are in danger," he said.

Geffray met with student representatives and trade unions later on Friday. After this meeting, student group leaders renewed their call for "concrete" responses to their demands, said the protests should continue, but also appealed to demonstrators to refrain from any violence or vandalism.

"If I could address a clear message to high schoolers: be smart. We are giving, once again, cause to those who wish to instrumentalize and discredit our cause. Be non-violent," Nahanael Combary of the Renouveau Lycéen group said.

Government blames far-left LFI

According to Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu, French domestic intelligence agencies told a crisis meeting on Thursday that the movement has been instrumentalized by politicians from the left-wing party La France Insoumise (France Unbowed or LFI) – who have denied the allegations.

Veteran LFI leader and 2027 presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon has indeed supported the protests but called on students to use non-violent methods.

"Students, teachers and educational staff are facing the same state of neglect and their positions and claims should be respected," he wrote in a statement earlier this week, calling for "disciplined struggle, no panic, no irritation."

Meanwhile, student union bodies have called for a day of mass protest next Tuesday, October 6, under the slogan: "Police out of schools! No to the repression of student mobilization!"

"The police have no place in front of educational establishments," read a statement. "We support the ongoing mobilization and call for it to be reinforced."

Edited by: Karl Sexton

entries.title: FlyDubai 'hero' pilot speaks for first time
entries.summary: India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi spoke with Captain Smit Machchhar via video call. Meanwhile, authorities in the UAE and Israel said an investigation is making progress.
entries.content:
United Arab Emirates

Flydubai 'hero' pilot speaks for first time

October 2, 2026

India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi spoke with Captain Smit Machchhar via video call. Meanwhile, authorities in the UAE and Israel said an investigation is making progress.

The Indian Flydubai pilot who was stabbed by his copilot in an apparent attempt to crash the plane has spoken about his ordeal for the first time.

After being seriously wounded, Captain Smit Machchhar managed to unlock the cockpit door. This enabled other passengers to enter the cockpit and restrain the copilot, while a deadheading pilot took control of the aircraft.

"I had so many wounds. I had fallen down," Machchhar told Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi via video call from his hospital bed in Abu Dhabi. "I was fighting for my life. At one point, I realized that if I didn’t get up … then passengers would lose their lives."

Some 180 passengers were on board the flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv, which was diverted to Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, due to the situation. Most passengers were Israeli nationals.

Anwar Gargash, an adviser to the UAE president, took to social media on Friday to say Machchhar deserved "the highest recognition for embodying courage and responsibility in the face of a terrorist act and an imminent catastrophe," all while calling him a "true hero."

The suspected attacker, an Omani national, was arrested upon landing in Saudi Arabia, with the motive still being unclear, with Israel saying it believes it was an attempted Islamist attack.

Official labels incident 'terrorist act'

A senior official from the United Arab Emirates on Friday labeled the incident as a terrorist attack. Israel used similar terms to describe the incident.

Flydubai CEO Ghaith Al Ghaith said the company will carry out a full investigation of the incident.

"It is important that we allow this process to establish the facts," he said in a statement.

The company said it will suspend its flights to Tel Aviv until at least October 15.

Israeli officials to investigate suspect: report

A source also told Reuters that Israeli officials are expected to investigate the flight's co-pilot, currently held in the UAE. The source emphasized it was the UAE who's responsible for the investigation.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the country was looking into whether the co-pilot had been instructed by anyone. 

"Whoever sent him will pay a very heavy price, Netanyahu said.

Netanyahu said the suspect had gone through "Islamist radical indoctrination," adding it was clear the man was "suicidal."

Many Israelis were stranded in the UAE as a result of the flight suspension between the two countries following the incident, with Israeli airlines receiving the necessary approvals to start repatriating Israeli nationals back to Israel.

Edited by: Zac Crellin

entries.title: Spain's parliament rejects housing bill as protests continue
entries.summary: Spain's minority government suffered defeat in parliament as it tried to push through a pair of emergency measures aimed at making housing more affordable. A pensioner's eviction and protests led to the bid.
entries.content:
Spain

Spain's parliament rejects housing bill as protests continue

October 2, 2026

Spain's minority government suffered defeat in parliament as it tried to push through a pair of emergency measures aimed at making housing more affordable. A pensioner's eviction and protests led to the bid.

Spain's parliament has narrowly voted down a pair of emergency government decrees aiming to quell widespread protests against rising rental costs for housing.

Hundreds of protesters were gathered outside the parliament in Madrid amid the marathon debate culminating in a pair of votes on Friday. They yelled "shame" and "your profits, our misery," as news of the measures being quashed filtered through.

Spain has been gripped by protests for around a week, including a tent city set up in central Madrid, ignited by the eviction of an 87-year-old pensioner from her apartment that threw the more longstanding issue of unaffordable housing costs into sharp focus.

Why and how did the emergency decrees fail?

Left-leaning Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez leads a minority government in Spain and so relies on opposition support to legislate. 

Sanchez spoke at the close of a marathon 5-hour debate in the Chamber of Deputies ahead of the vote, urging members: "Do the right thing, or history will judge you, and sooner than you think."

One Catalan party that sometimes supports Sanchez's government, the economically right-leaning Junts group, joined the opposition in voting down the measures.

The first emergency decree, which the government said would stop evictions of vulnerable people, make real estate speculation harder and provide tax incentives to encourage renting, failed by a narrow margin of 178-172.

The second decree, which sought to make residential leases automatically renewable by tenants, fell further short of a majority at 184-166.

Opponents to the measures argued, among other things, that they risked compounding the situation by reducing housing supply.

Some also argued that Sanchez should respond to the deadlock by calling early elections, possibly initiating a wholesale change of government.

What did protesters say after the vote?

The Tenants' Union which had led protests across Spain said it would press on with plans for more mass rallies on Saturday, aiming to continue heaping pressure on the coalition and opposition alike.

"The encampment will continue and will continue expanding to other neighborhoods," Tenants' Union spokesperson Alicia del Rio said. "We're aiming for a general strike."

The current wave of protests, albeit concerning an issue that's been bubbling away near the surface for years, was triggered by the high-profile eviction of 87-year-old Madrid resident Maricarmen Abascal from the apartment she had occupied for almost all of her life.

How tough is Spain's housing market?

The investment company owning Abascal's building reversed the measure in her case this week but only after the issue had become a symbol of growing frustration of housing costs.

Rents have roughly doubled in Spain in the last decade and young people, facing one of Europe's toughest labor markets for school-leavers and graduates, frequently live with their parents past the age of 30.

"People have said 'enough is enough;' this ⁠cannot ​go on. The housing problem must be resolved; structural measures must be taken, and this cannot ​continue," Abascal's lawyer, Beatriz Duro, said in an interview with Reuters on Thursday.

The next step after Friday's failed vote in parliament is difficult to identify. Sanchez has so far ruled out calling early elections. He could try to formulate another emergency decree or decrees in response to the protests, but any such move would need to overcome the same hurdles in parliament.

Edited by: Zac Crellin

entries.title: "NAZA": Israeli military issues statement on film
entries.summary: The award-winning documentary "NAZA" continues to spark controversy in Israel. The Israeli military has now published a multi-page statement calling the film's portrayal "distorted."
entries.content:
Israel

Israeli military rejects allegations portrayed in 'NAZA'

October 2, 2026

The award-winning documentary "NAZA" continues to spark controversy in Israel. The Israeli military has now published a multi-page statement calling the film's portrayal "distorted."

When it premiered at the Venice International Film Festival in mid-September, "NAZA" received a 25-minute-long standing ovation and the Special Jury Prize. But in Israel, the documentary has fueled heated debate.

Israeli Culture Minister Miki Zohar described the work of filmmakers Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham "treason against the state" and urged that their citizenship be revoked. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has also sharply criticized the documentary.

Now the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) has also rejected the film's allegations about its conduct during the war in Gaza. In a multi-page document, the military accuses the filmmakers of presenting a "distorted, misleading and disingenuous picture." The film, it says, is based on "substantial factual errors" resulting from "manipulative misrepresentations of reality." 

An insider's look at the war

The 80-minute documentary examines the Israel Defense Forces' operations during the war in Gaza. It is based on interviews conducted with 24 anonymous military and intelligence personnel, who describe internal procedures and decision-making processes involved in selecting targets in the Gaza Strip. According to the interviewees, high civilian casualty estimates were, in some cases, deliberately factored into these decisions. 

The IDF rejects those claims. It says it has never planned or carried out attacks while anticipating hundreds of civilian deaths. It also disputes the film's claim that artificial intelligence selected targets without human oversight, saying people have always made decisions about targets and attacks.

The military also accuses the filmmakers of omitting important facts. According to the IDF, the film fails to show the role of military legal advisors and commanders in reviewing and authorizing attacks or the measures it says it takes to protect civilians. It also argues that the film does not adequately address the Hamas attacks on Israel on October 7, 2023, in which over 1,200 people were killed and 250 people were taken hostage. 

Several human rights organizations and a UN commission have accused Israel of committing acts of genocide in Gaza. According to health authorities in Gaza and other sources, at least 74,000 Palestinians have been killed since the war began. 

'NAZA' opens in theaters worldwide

Speaking at the awards ceremony in Venice in mid-September, co-director Yuval Abraham said: "We believe that the denial of a crime is what helps it persist. That is why it's really, really especially important to us that Israelis watch this film."

Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham also worked on the film "No Other Land," which won an Oscar for Best Documentary Feature in 2025. 

"NAZA" comes from the Hebrew term "Nezek Agavi," meaning collateral damage. According to a soldier interviewed in the film, the acronym is used within the military to refer to the estimated number of civilians who could be killed in an attack.

Numerous human rights organizations, including the Israeli group B'Tselem, have expressed their support for the filmmakers. After its world premiere at the Venice Film Festival, "NAZA" is now showing in theaters worldwide.

This article was originally published in German.
